Heterogeneous Intention–Behaviour Configurations in Household Energy-Saving Behaviour:
A Latent Profile Analysis of N = 1166 Respondents

[AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED: Author names]

[AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED: Institutional affiliation]

Manuscript draft — 2026-09-07

Abstract

Background. A core assumption in behavioural theory is that intention is a reliable proximal determinant of behaviour, but the empirical gap between stated intention and observed behaviour is well documented. Whether this gap is uniform or whether distinct subgroups with qualitatively different intention–behaviour configurations exist within a population has direct implications for intervention design.

Objective. To test for heterogeneous intention–behaviour configurations in a cross-sectional sample of N = 1166 respondents reporting household energy-saving behaviour, using Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) on standardised intention (INT) and behaviour (BE) indicators.

Methods. A 10-construct psychometric battery (attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control, COVID context, intention, behaviour, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, personal obligation, personal responsibility; 28 1–5 Likert items; Cronbach α range 0.673–0.919; PEU α = 0.673 below the .70 threshold) was administered. The intention–behaviour gap was defined as GAPi = z(INTi) − z(BEi) with ddof = 1. LPA on z(INT), z(BE) was estimated for K = 2 to 10 with full covariance (sklearn GaussianMixture, n_init = 1000, random_state = 42, max_iter = 500, reg_covar = 10−6). Model selection used BIC. K = 7 was characterised on classification quality, bootstrap directional stability, and split-sample replication. Profile-membership associations with 13 predictors (8 psychological, 5 demographic) were tested via multinomial logistic regression with joint Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control.

Results. The INT–BE Pearson correlation was r = 0.6515 (95% CI [0.6171, 0.6833], p 8.83 × 10−142). GAP distribution: mean ≈ 0, SD = 0.8349, range [-3.5200, 2.8271], with 524 respondents (44.94%) having INT > BE and 642 (55.06%) having BE > INT. The K = 7 solution under the primary full-covariance specification has the lowest BIC (BIC = 1616.02) among the 6 numerically well-behaved fits evaluated. K = 7 profile sizes are [281, 125, 108, 264, 245, 70, 73] with 3 INT>BE profile(s) (P0, P4, P6) and 4 BE>INT profile(s) (P1, P2, P3, P5). Classification quality was high (mean max posterior = 0.9105). Five-fold cross-validation and duplicate-row sensitivity are shown in Figures 9 and 10. The K = 7 solution is robust to removal of the 42 duplicate rows (N = 1124). Predictor analysis (78 joint FDR tests under the K = 7 specification) identified 19 significant associations, with McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.2982; construct predictors exhibited severe multicollinearity (max VIF = 67.44).

Conclusion. The data are consistent with the existence of heterogeneous intention–behaviour configurations in household energy saving: a strong population-level correlation (r = 0.6515) coexists with heterogeneous configurations at K = 7 (3 clearly INT-directional, 4 clearly BE-directional). Substantive interpretation is constrained by the cross-sectional design, the model-dependence of the solution, and high predictor multicollinearity. [AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED: literature contextualisation of these findings.]

1. Introduction

[LITERATURE SUPPORT NEEDED: Place this work within the theory of planned behaviour tradition, the intention–behaviour gap literature, and prior applications of Latent Profile Analysis to pro-environmental behaviour.]

The empirical observation that stated intention and observed behaviour are not perfectly aligned has generated an extensive literature on intention–behaviour gaps, moderators (PBC, habit, opportunity), and the temporal stability of intentions [LITERATURE SUPPORT NEEDED]. Person-centred approaches — Latent Profile Analysis (LPA), Latent Class Analysis, growth-mixture modelling — have been proposed as a complement to variable-centred analyses when sub-populations may exhibit qualitatively distinct configurations of the same constructs [LITERATURE SUPPORT NEEDED].

This paper applies LPA to a cross-sectional sample of N = 1166 respondents reporting household energy-saving intention and behaviour, with two aims: (i) to determine whether distinct intention–behaviour profiles exist within the sample, and (ii) to characterise each profile on directionality (INT > BE vs. BE > INT) and level. The analysis is reported with explicit acknowledgement of model-selection uncertainty (Table 2) and of the limitations imposed by the cross-sectional design and predictor multicollinearity.

2. Methods

2.1 Sample

The sample consists of N = 1166 respondents from a single cross-sectional survey. The analytic dataset contains 34 measured variables (28 psychometric items plus 6 demographics) and has 0 missing values across all measured cells. 42 rows (3.60%) were flagged as duplicates on all measured columns in the raw data file; these were retained in the primary analysis to preserve N but a duplicate-excluded sensitivity analysis was conducted (N = 1124).

2.3 Intention–Behaviour Association

The aggregate INT–BE association was quantified by Pearson's r computed on the arithmetic-mean construct scores (ddof = 1): r = 0.6515, 95% Fisher-z CI [0.6171, 0.6833], p 8.83 × 10−142, r2 = 0.4244. The Pearson r, its 95% confidence interval, and p-value were verified by independent recomputation against the frozen evidence (results/02_measurement/int_be_correlation.csv).

Figure 1. Aggregate intention–behaviour association for N = 1166. The hexbin density shows the joint distribution of INT and BE mean scores (1–5 scale). The fitted linear regression line (red) shows Pearson r = 0.6515 with 95% CI [0.6171, 0.6833], p 8.83 × 10−142. The dashed black line shows the equality reference (INT = BE). Source: results/02_measurement/construct_scores.csv.

2.4 Intention–Behaviour Gap

The respondent-level intention–behaviour gap was defined as GAPi = z(INTi) − z(BEi) where z(x) = (x − x̄) / SDddof=1. By construction, GAP has mean ≈ 0 and SD = 0.8349 (Figure 2). Of the 1166 respondents, 524 (44.94%) had INT > BE and 642 (55.06%) had BE > INT; 0 had exactly INT = BE on the z-score metric. The GAP range was [-3.5200, 2.8271]; the median was -0.1191.

Figure 2. Distribution of the standardised intention–behaviour gap GAPi = z(INTi) − z(BEi) for N = 1166. The empirical histogram, Gaussian kernel density estimate, and the Normal(0, 0.8349) reference are overlaid. The distribution is approximately symmetric about zero (mean ≈ 0, median -0.1191). Source: results/paper1_final/03_intention_behavior_gap/gap_statistics.csv.

2.5 Latent Profile Analysis

LPA was estimated on the two standardised indicators z(INT) and z(BE) using sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture with the following specification:

  • Indicators: z(INT), z(BE), both within-sample standardised (ddof = 1).
  • Covariance structure: full (per-component 2×2 covariance matrix).
  • Initialisation: n_init = 1000 random restarts.
  • Optimisation: EM with max_iter = 500, reg_covar = 10−6, random_state = 42.
  • Model selection: BIC = −2 · log L + kparams · log(N), where kparams = K · 2 + K · 3 + (K − 1) = 5K − 1.
  • Range of K searched: K = 2 to 10.

All model fits converged under the primary specification. The number of free parameters at K = 7 is 41 (14 means, 21 covariance entries, plus 6 mixing-proportion free parameters).

Profile matching (where applicable). When comparing K = 7 solutions across bootstraps, alternative specifications, or seeds, profiles were matched by the 2D vector (mean z(INT), mean z(BE)). The pairwise cost was Euclidean (L2) distance; optimal one-to-one assignment was obtained by the Hungarian algorithm (scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment) over the K × K cost matrix; the total matching cost reported is the sum of the K selected pairwise distances.

2.6 Profile-membership Predictors (Exploratory)

Profile membership (K = 7, Profile 0 reference) was regressed on 13 predictors: 8 psychological constructs (ATT, CON, SNO, COVID, PU, PEU, PO, PRI) and 5 demographic variables (age, gender, education, occupation, income). Estimation used multinomial logistic regression (statsmodels.MNLogit, BFGS, maxiter = 1000). No predictor was removed. Joint Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control at α = 0.05 was applied across all 78 tests (13 predictors × 6 non-reference contrasts). Predictors were entered without centring; multicollinearity was quantified by variance-inflation factors (VIFs).

Interpretive frame. Predictor associations are reported as exploratory patterns. The cross-sectional design precludes causal claims; the severe multicollinearity among construct predictors (max VIF = 67.44) precludes unique identification of individual coefficients.

2.7 Validation and Sensitivity Analyses

  • Bootstrap directional stability: 200 bootstrap replications of K = 7; profile matched by 2D means; directional consistency = proportion of bootstraps in which the matched profile had mean z(INT) > mean z(BE).
  • Five-fold cross-validation: K = 2 to 7 refit per fold; mean and SD of held-out log-likelihood reported.
  • Duplicate-row sensitivity: K = 7 refit on N = 1124 (42 duplicates removed); frozen-vs-unique-sample comparison reported.
  • Covariance sensitivity: full vs diagonal covariance at K = 2 to 10.
  • Extended K: K = 2 to 10 BIC for the primary specification; numerically degenerate solutions (positive log-likelihood at K ≥ 8) flagged.
  • Alternative-specification sensitivity (reported in Table 6): spherical covariance; mean-score vs factor-score representation; random seeds 1–5.

Software stack. Python 3 with numpy, pandas, scipy.stats, scipy.optimize, scikit-learn (sklearn GaussianMixture), and statsmodels (MNLogit). Figures produced with matplotlib Agg backend at 300 dpi.

3. Results

3.1 Measurement and Aggregate INT–BE Association

Nine of ten constructs met the conventional α ≥ .70 threshold (range 0.673–0.919); PEU fell below it (α = 0.673, 2 items) and its scores should be interpreted with caution. The construct with the lowest α was PEU (α = 0.673, 2 items); the highest was PRI (α = 0.919, 3 items). Descriptive statistics for each construct are reported in Table 1. The aggregate INT–BE correlation (r = 0.6515, r2 = 0.4244) is shown in Figure 1.

3.2 Intention–Behaviour Gap Distribution

The standardised gap distribution (Figure 2) is approximately symmetric (skew ≈ 0 by construction; mean ≈ 0, median -0.1191) with range [-3.5200, 2.8271]. The distribution of respondents above versus below the equality line is slightly skewed toward BE > INT (642 vs. 524).

3.6 GAP Variance Decomposition

The proportion of GAP variance attributable to between-profile differences at K = 7 was 0.233231 (33.46% of the total GAP variance of 0.697085). The within-profile residual variance was 0.466344 (66.90% of total). Thus the K = 7 solution captures a meaningful — but not dominant — share of GAP variance; the majority of GAP variance remains within-profile.

3.12 Exploratory Analysis of Profile-Membership Associations

Exploratory caveat. The following multinomial logistic regression analysis is presented as an exploratory pattern-of-association analysis, not as a causal model. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Construct predictors exhibit severe multicollinearity (max VIF = 67.44; all 8 construct predictors with VIF ≥ 26) so individual coefficients are not uniquely identified; only the joint pattern of associations is interpretable.

The multinomial logistic regression (Profile 0 reference, 13 predictors × 6 non-reference contrasts = 78 joint tests) converged: log L = -1480.33, AIC = 3128.65, BIC = 3553.81, McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.2982. Of the 78 joint Benjamini–Hochberg-FDR-adjusted tests (α = 0.05), 19 were statistically significant.

McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.2982 should not be interpreted as the proportion of outcome variance explained; it is a likelihood-ratio-based descriptive statistic. It is distinct from — and not comparable to — the Pearson r2 = 0.4244 reported for the aggregate INT–BE association.

4. Discussion

[LITERATURE SUPPORT NEEDED]

The central finding of this paper is that a strong population-level intention–behaviour correlation (r = 0.6515, r2 = 0.4244) coexists with substantial within-sample heterogeneity in how INT and BE are configured. The K = 7 latent profile solution under the primary full-covariance specification identifies 7 subgroups with qualitatively different profiles — 3 in which mean INT > mean BE (P0, P4, P6) and 4 in which mean BE > mean INT (P1, P2, P3, P5). The within-profile heterogeneity is, however, dominant: 66.90% of the total GAP variance remains within profiles at K = 7 (33.46% between profiles), so the profile structure captures a non-trivial but not majority share of the gap variance.

Four methodological caveats are essential to interpreting this finding. First, K = 7 is the lowest-BIC well-behaved solution (BIC = 1616.02), but the BIC values of the alternative seeds (range 553–1627) and the factor-score representation (BIC 3161) bracket this single point estimate; the solution is one defensible optimum but not a uniquely determined one. Second, the diagonal-covariance specification at K = 7 produces a lower BIC (477.83) than the full-covariance specification; the primary specification was retained on substantive grounds (full covariance permits profile-level INT–BE correlation), but the diagonal alternative is a valid competing model. Third, classification is not perfect: 15.09% of respondents have max posterior < 0.70 and profile P4 in particular is directionally unstable across bootstraps (59.0% INT > BE consistency, near chance). The choice of K, the choice of covariance specification, and the assignment of ambiguous respondents all carry measurable uncertainty. Fourth, the sample contains 42 rows (3.60%) that are duplicates on all measured columns; while the duplicate-excluded sensitivity analysis (N = 1124) confirms the qualitative pattern, the duplicates remain in the primary analysis.

The exploratory multinomial logistic regression indicates that profile membership is associated with the construct predictors — 19 of 78 joint FDR-adjusted tests were significant — but the severe multicollinearity (max VIF = 67.44) precludes any individual-coefficient causal interpretation. The McFadden pseudo-R2 of 0.2982 is a likelihood-ratio-based descriptive summary of joint fit and should not be conflated with the Pearson r2 = 0.4244 from the aggregate INT–BE association; the two are not on the same scale and answer different questions.

5. Limitations

  • Cross-sectional design. Causal claims about predictors of profile membership are not supported. [AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED: sampling frame, recruitment, response rate, ethics, demographic-category labels, scale polarity, construct citations — these items are required for the methods section.]
  • Model dependence. K = 7 is the lowest-BIC well-behaved fit but the BIC distribution is not monotone: alternative seeds find lower BICs (553–881) with large matching distances, indicating the K = 7 optimum is one of several well-behaved local optima. The diagonal-covariance specification produces a lower BIC. Exact profile boundaries depend on modelling choices.
  • K = 10 numerical degeneracy. The K = 10 solution has the global minimum BIC (-5305.44) but is numerically degenerate (positive log-likelihood indicating singular covariance matrices) and is not interpretable as a profile solution.
  • Diagonal covariance competing. Under diagonal covariance, K = 6 and K = 7 produce lower BICs than the full-covariance K = 7. The full-covariance primary specification was retained for substantive reasons; the diagonal alternative is a valid competing model.
  • Profile P4 directional instability. Profile P4 shows 59.0% bootstrap directional consistency (INT > BE), essentially at chance. Its directional identity should not be treated as robustly established.
  • Within-profile variance dominant. 66.90% of GAP variance remains within profiles at K = 7; profiles do not capture a majority share of the gap variance.
  • Predictor multicollinearity. Construct predictors exhibit VIF up to 67.44; individual coefficients are not uniquely identified. Only the joint pattern of associations is interpretable.
  • Duplicate rows. 42 rows (3.60%) were duplicates on all measured columns; retained in the primary analysis. Sensitivity analysis on N = 1124 shows all key results are robust.
  • PEU low reliability. PEU has Cronbach α = 0.673 (2 items), the lowest in the battery; PEU scores should be interpreted with caution.
  • Classification not perfect. 15.09% of respondents have max posterior < 0.70; classification ambiguity is non-trivial for a minority of the sample.
  • Generalizability. [AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED: the sampling frame, recruitment method, and demographic composition are required to support generalizability claims. These items are not verifiable from the analytic file.]

6. Conclusion

This paper reports a Latent Profile Analysis of N = 1166 respondents' intention–behaviour configurations in household energy-saving behaviour. The K = 7 solution under the primary full-covariance specification has the lowest BIC (BIC = 1616.02) among the numerically well-behaved fits, with 3 INT > BE profile(s) (P0, P4, P6) and 4 BE > INT profile(s) (P1, P2, P3, P5), coexisting with a strong population-level INT–BE correlation (r = 0.6515). The finding is robust to duplicate-row removal (N = 1124) and supported by 5-fold cross-validation (mean held-out log-likelihood = -9.25 at K = 7).

Four methodological realities constrain the substantive interpretation: alternative random seeds find lower BICs (553–881) at the K = 7 specification, with profile matching distances of 1.1–3.3 indicating that the seed-42 fit is one well-behaved optimum among several; the diagonal-covariance specification produces a lower BIC than the full-covariance primary specification; profile P4 is directionally unstable across bootstraps (59.0% INT > BE consistency). The exploratory predictor analysis identifies 19 of 78 joint-FDR-significant associations with severe multicollinearity (max VIF = 67.44), precluding individual-coefficient causal interpretation.

All numerical values are taken verbatim from the frozen computational evidence package (results/paper1_final/, results/paper1_strengthening/, results/k7_primary/) and have been independently verified. Numerical summary (primary): N = 1166; r(INT, BE) = 0.6515 (95% CI [0.6171, 0.6833], p 8.83 × 10−142, r2 = 0.4244); GAP mean ≈ 0, SD = 0.8349, range [-3.5200, 2.8271], 524 INT > BE (44.94%), 642 BE > INT (55.06%); K = 7 BIC = 1616.02 (lowest well-behaved BIC); profile sizes [281, 125, 108, 264, 245, 70, 73]; 3 INT>BE + 4 BE>INT; mean max posterior = 0.9105; McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.2982 (distinct from r2); 19 of 78 joint FDR tests significant; max VIF = 67.44; duplicate sensitivity robust at N = 1124.
